questions.prompt: A realization of a transfer function \(G(s)\) is
questions.explanation: Many state-space models share one transfer function. A change of state basis produces another realization of the same \(G\). There is no unique quadruple \((A,B,C,D)\). The inverse is a different system. Poles alone do not fix the zeros or the gain.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 234 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a transfer function as one block</title><text x="24" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">in</text><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="78" y2="56"/><polygon points="78,56 71.6,58.7 71.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="78" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="120" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">G</text><line x1="162" y1="56" x2="198" y2="56"/><polygon points="198,56 191.6,58.7 191.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="202" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">out</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A single block labeled as the plant.
options: any state-space model whose input-output map is \(G(s)\)
the unique set of matrices \(A, B, C, D\) that can ever represent \(G\)
a list of the poles with the zeros thrown away

questions.prompt: \(G(s) = 8/(s+2)\) has no cancellation. A minimal realization uses this many states:
questions.explanation: The denominator degree is 1, so the minimal state dimension is 1. A two-state model would hide a cancelled mode. The numerator 8 is a gain, not a state count.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>one real pole</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One pole mark on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: \(G(s) = (s+3)/(s^2 + 7s + 10)\) has no cancellation. A minimal realization uses this many states:
questions.explanation: The denominator is degree 2 and nothing cancels, so the minimal dimension is 2. The single zero does not reduce the state count. A first-order model would drop a pole.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two real poles</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="26" y2="90"/><line x1="54" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="85" x2="45" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="95" x2="45" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: In controllable canonical form, the denominator \(s^2 + 4s + 5\) puts \(-a_0\) in the bottom-left entry of \(A\). That entry is
questions.explanation: \(a_0 = 5\), so the bottom-left entry is \(-5\), stored as -5. The coefficient \(a_1 = 4\) belongs in the bottom-right entry, with a minus sign, as \(-4\). Using \(+5\) drops the sign in the companion matrix.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>controllable companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-a0   -a1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A companion matrix with a symbolic last row.

questions.prompt: If \(x = Tz\) with \(T\) invertible, the new realization has
questions.explanation: A change of basis preserves the input-output map and replaces \(A\) by \(T^{-1}AT\), or \(TAT^{-1}\), depending on which way \(T\) is defined. The entries of \(A\) change unless \(T\) is trivial. The poles stay the eigenvalues of \(A\), not the eigenvalues of \(T\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>controllable companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-a0   -a1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A companion matrix with a symbolic last row.
options: a different transfer function and a similar \(A\)
the same transfer function, and an \(A\) matrix similar to the old one
the same \(A\) matrix, entry by entry
new poles, equal to the eigenvalues of \(T\)

questions.prompt: \(G(s) = 6(s+1)/((s+1)(s+3))\) cancels to a first-order system. The DC gain of that minimal model is
questions.explanation: After cancelling \(s+1\), \(G(s) = 6/(s+3)\) and \(G(0) = 6/3 = 2\). The uncancelled expression at \(s = 0\) is also \(6/3 = 2\), so the cancellation does not change the gain. The state count 1 is the order, not the DC gain.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 234 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a transfer function as one block</title><text x="24" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">in</text><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="78" y2="56"/><polygon points="78,56 71.6,58.7 71.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="78" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="120" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">G</text><line x1="162" y1="56" x2="198" y2="56"/><polygon points="198,56 191.6,58.7 191.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="202" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">out</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A single block labeled as the plant.

questions.prompt: Observable canonical form, compared with controllable canonical form of the same \(G(s)\),
questions.explanation: The two companion forms are transposes of each other, up to the way \(B\) and \(C\) carry the numerator. They realize the same \(G\) and therefore have the same poles. Zeros are allowed in both forms; they move into \(C\) or into \(B\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>controllable companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-a0   -a1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A companion matrix with a symbolic last row.
options: is the transpose structure: the coefficients run down a column instead of along the last row
exists only when \(G\) has no zeros

questions.explanation: \(G(0) = 9/18 = 0.5\). The ratio of the leading coefficients, \(3/1 = 3\), is the high-frequency behavior of a relative-degree-1 system only after dividing by \(s\), not the DC gain. The pole sum 4 is the coefficient of \(s\), not \(G(0)\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 234 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a transfer function as one block</title><text x="24" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">in</text><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="78" y2="56"/><polygon points="78,56 71.6,58.7 71.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="78" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="120" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">G</text><line x1="162" y1="56" x2="198" y2="56"/><polygon points="198,56 191.6,58.7 191.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="202" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">out</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A controllable companion matrix is \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\). In \(s^2 + a_1 s + a_0\), the coefficient \(a_1\) is
questions.explanation: The last row is \((-a_0,\; -a_1) = (-2,\; -7)\), so \(a_1 = 7\). The constant term \(a_0\) is 2. The trace of \(A\) is \(-7\), which is \(-a_1\), not \(a_1\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a numerical companion matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-2   -7</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A companion matrix with a numerical last row.

questions.prompt: \(G(s) = (s+4)/((s+4)(s+1)(s+6))\) has one cancellation. A minimal realization uses this many states:
questions.explanation: The written denominator has degree 3 and one factor cancels, leaving degree 2. The minimal state count is 2. Keeping all three poles counts a hidden mode. Cancelling and then dropping a second pole would leave a first-order model of the wrong system.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two real poles</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="26" y2="90"/><line x1="54" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="85" x2="45" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="95" x2="45" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: A non-minimal realization hides a mode. That mode is
questions.explanation: Cancellation means the hidden eigenvalue does not appear in \(G(s)\). The mode is unreachable, unobservable, or both. It need not be the slowest mode. An extra zero that does not cancel is visible and does not by itself add a hidden state. Every pole of a realization's transfer function is an eigenvalue; the hidden ones are the eigenvalues that are not poles.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two real poles</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="26" y2="90"/><line x1="54" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="85" x2="45" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="35" y1="95" x2="45" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks on the negative real axis.
options: always slower than every pole of \(G(s)\)
visible in the transfer function as an extra zero that does not cancel
a pole of \(G(s)\) that was never an eigenvalue
either unreachable or unobservable, which is why it cancels

questions.prompt: The denominator \(s^2 + 9s + 14\) is written in controllable canonical form. The determinant of \(A\), which equals \(a_0\), is
questions.explanation: For the companion matrix, \(\det A = a_0 = 14\). The coefficient 9 is \(a_1\), which is minus the trace, not the determinant. The product of the two coefficients is not \(a_0\).
